title: Generative AI Asks Teachers to Eat Scraps From the Table
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer argues that technologies are rarely built for teachers, so teachers receive generative AI as scraps from the table of commerce and must decide whether it can become a meal. To do that, anyone working with AI in learning needs two guides: a theory of technology and a theory of learning, and he finds that boosters can explain the first crisply but mumble on the second. He tests three examples, including Khan Academy's tolerance of hallucinations, chatbot conversations with historical figures, and children's personalised virtual twins, and shows that each implies a theory of learning that does not hold up. Novices cannot critique wrong answers, expert content knowledge differs from teaching knowledge, and a tutor that echoes a child's pessimism about math reinforces rather than develops her ideas. The piece closes with a plain call to demand a meal rather than eat the scraps, and with his prediction that AI will not transform education in five years.
points: Evaluate any classroom AI claim with two questions: what makes the technology powerful and how people actually learn.
Hallucinations cannot benefit novices because a novice lacks the expertise needed to catch the errors.
Great historical figures or subject experts are not necessarily good teachers; pedagogical content knowledge is its own specialised body of knowledge.
A personalised tutor that mirrors a child's views strengthens misconceptions, while school deliberately brings different people together to challenge them.
Meyer expects modest quality-of-life gains for teachers, not transformation, in the near term.
quotes: If you want to do anything useful with generative AI in learning, you need to recruit two guides where most people in this space seem to only have one. You need a theory of technology, answering the questions, “What makes this technology powerful? Why and how do people use it?” And you need a theory of learning, answering the questions, “How do people learn? What do students want and need?
Generally, when people say, “Generative AI technology will transform learning,” they can tell you quite crisply how the technology works but will mumble if you ask them how learning works.

My theory of learning is that students come to class with ideas about every subject. Students need opportunities to express those ideas, to feel affirmed in the value of their ideas, and then to receive resources that help them develop their ideas. That’s the whole game.

But I cannot believe that these hallucinations are a benefit to novices in any way. A novice who needs Khanmigo by definition does not have access to the knowledge that an expert would use to critique Khamigo.

The need to experience people less like us is a huge reason why we do school. We bring different kids and grownups together in schools intentionally—not by accident, convenience, or financial necessity. When different people share contrasting views of a thing, it often helps everyone understand that thing better than any one of them could on their own.

If you are a teacher and do not have a concrete theory of learning, you will succumb too easily to a marketing campaign that is without precedent in my lifetime, a campaign designed to convince you that generative AI’s transformation of learning is inevitable, designed to convince you that these scraps falling from the table of commerce are, in fact, a multi-course meal. Your theory of learning will tell you whether or not they’re right.

Generative AI will not transform education in the next five years. AI won’t change any of the ways students learn—including how we organize and resource them, how we staff their schools, how their achievement sorts into different distributions—in any appreciable way over the next five years. If pressed I’d guess much longer.
